members.name: Nonverbal Dominance
members.source_definition: Using body language, sighs, eye rolls, stares, or physical presence to intimidate, dismiss, or control without words.

approved_draft.why_this_matters: Because nothing quotable is ever said, the experience cannot be evidenced to anyone else, and the person on the receiving end often ends up self-editing around a reaction they could not describe if asked.
approved_draft.what_it_is_not: Faces move on their own: a flash of visible irritation, an expressive manner, a real sigh at the end of a long day. Ask whether the reaction appears whenever something is annoying, or specifically whenever one person disagrees.

existing_specific_text.short_definition: Using body language, sighs, eye rolls, stares, or physical presence to intimidate, dismiss, or control without words.
existing_specific_text.expanded_definition: Using body language — sighs, eye rolls, prolonged stares, an imposing physical presence — to intimidate, dismiss, or control without ever saying anything that could be directly quoted or held accountable. The message is unmistakable to the target while remaining fully deniable to anyone else.
existing_specific_text.plain_language_summary: In plain terms: using body language, sighs, eye rolls, stares, or physical presence to intimidate, dismiss, or control without words.
existing_specific_text.why_this_matters: Patterns like this can shape communication, trust, and decision-making — left unnamed, they can contribute to practical entrapment — the cost of leaving or objecting keeps rising the longer it continues. Naming a pattern accurately — without over-claiming — is usually what restores clarity faster than either ignoring it or catastrophizing it.
what_it_is: Using body language, sighs, eye rolls, stares, or physical presence to intimidate, dismiss, or control without words.
what_it_sounds_like: A pointed sigh, eye roll, or exaggerated exhale specifically timed to a moment the target speaks up or disagrees.
Prolonged, uncomfortable staring used to communicate displeasure or force a topic to be dropped, with no words exchanged.
The target finds themselves self-editing to avoid triggering a nonverbal reaction, even though nothing was ever explicitly said.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Genuine, involuntary emotional reactions are a normal part of being human and aren't automatically a control tactic. Some people are naturally more expressive in their face and body language, without any intent to intimidate.
common_false_positives: Genuine, involuntary reactions (a startled expression, real frustration shown briefly) that aren't calculated to intimidate.
A person's naturally expressive face or body language that isn't targeted at controlling anyone.
A one-off, honest reaction to something genuinely frustrating, not a recurring pattern used specifically around disagreement.
discernment_questions: Does the nonverbal reaction happen specifically and reliably around moments of disagreement or boundary-setting?
Does the target notice themselves self-editing specifically to avoid triggering it?
Would a neutral observer read the body language as intended to intimidate or dismiss, or as an ordinary, involuntary reaction?
Does this happen as a recurring pattern, or was it a single, honest reaction to something genuinely frustrating?
less_concerning_if: The reaction is involuntary, occasional, and doesn't specifically cluster around disagreement or boundaries.
more_concerning_if: The nonverbal reaction reliably and specifically follows disagreement, and the target self-edits to avoid it.
existing_specific_text.repair_check: After the incident, was there a genuine acknowledgment (not a non-apology), a concrete change in behavior, and no repeat of the same pattern? Repair is a pattern of change over time, not a single sentence of regret.
existing_specific_text.boundary_respect_check: When a boundary was stated plainly in this area, was it honored going forward — or tested, ignored, punished, or reframed as unreasonable? Boundary respect observed over multiple instances is one of the more reliable signals available.
existing_specific_text.psychological_mechanism: One documented mechanism behind patterns like this is that they can operate through concrete arrangements — money, contracts, timing — rather than anything said in the moment. This describes a possible mechanism, not a claim about what any specific person intended.
existing_specific_text.possible_impact_on_receiver: People sometimes describe practical entrapment — the cost of leaving or objecting keeps rising the longer it continues in connection with patterns like this. Impact varies widely by person, history, and context — this is a possibility to consider, not a predicted or universal outcome, and it is not a diagnosis of the person on the receiving end of a sustained pattern like this.

members.name: Postural Dominance
members.source_definition: Occupying higher-status physical positions to communicate authority through spatial hierarchy.

approved_draft.why_this_matters: Being physically talked down to registers below the level of argument; a sense of having shrunk arrives with nothing concrete to point at.
approved_draft.what_it_is_not: Rooms have layouts, people have different heights and builds, and someone standing up is usually just about to leave. What separates this from ordinary movement is positioning that recurs specifically around correction or disagreement.

existing_specific_text.short_definition: Occupying higher-status physical positions to communicate authority through spatial hierarchy.
existing_specific_text.expanded_definition: Deliberately occupying higher-status physical positions — standing while others sit, taking up more space than necessary, positioning at the head of a table — to communicate authority and hierarchy through spatial arrangement rather than words. This works because physical positioning carries real, largely unconscious social signaling about status and power.
existing_specific_text.plain_language_summary: In plain terms: occupying higher-status physical positions to communicate authority through spatial hierarchy.
existing_specific_text.why_this_matters: Patterns like this can shape communication, trust, and decision-making — left unnamed, they can contribute to practical entrapment — the cost of leaving or objecting keeps rising the longer it continues. what_it_is: Occupying higher-status physical positions to communicate authority through spatial hierarchy.
what_it_sounds_like: A consistent pattern of standing over someone who's seated, specifically during moments of disagreement or correction.
Physical space is consistently occupied in a way that visually diminishes the target's presence in the room.
The target notices a physical sense of being talked down to, quite literally, that seems to track moments of conflict.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Room layouts and practical circumstances often dictate physical positioning without anyone intending anything by it. A person's natural size or posture isn't a deliberate choice to dominate.
common_false_positives: Ordinary spatial arrangements dictated by a room's layout or the practicalities of a situation, not anyone's deliberate choice.
A person's natural size or posture, which isn't a deliberate choice to dominate space.
A brief, situational positioning (like standing to leave) that isn't a recurring, targeted pattern.

Is there a practical, non-strategic reason for the physical arrangement (room layout, task requirements)?

Would this positioning be noteworthy at all outside a context involving conflict or hierarchy?
less_concerning_if: The physical arrangement reflects practical circumstances rather than a targeted, recurring choice.
more_concerning_if: The positioning specifically and reliably tracks moments of disagreement or correction.

members.name: Fabricated Evidence
members.source_definition: Manufactured screenshots, edited messages, or forged documents presented as proof.

existing_specific_text.short_definition: Manufactured screenshots, edited messages, or forged documents presented as proof.
existing_specific_text.expanded_definition: Manufactured screenshots, edited messages, or forged documents presented as proof. As a communication pattern, Fabricated Evidence-type behavior in the Deception category tends to work by controlling what information the other person has access to, so their conclusions are built on an incomplete or false picture — describing a pattern in the exchange, not a fixed trait in the person. As a Reference-only, forensic entry, note: this is an evidence-and-reporting matter, not something this tool scores or verifies.
existing_specific_text.plain_language_summary: In plain terms: manufactured screenshots, edited messages, or forged documents presented as proof. If this is happening to you, the priority is evidence and reporting, not analysis.
existing_specific_text.why_this_matters: Patterns like this can shape communication, trust, and decision-making — left unnamed, they can contribute to misplaced trust in a distorted picture of a situation, discovered later, if at all. Recognizing this category matters because the right response (evidence, reporting) is different from the right response to an ordinary conflict.
what_it_is: Manufactured screenshots, edited messages, or forged documents presented as proof.
Recognizable by phrasing such as "'Receipts' of things you never wrote, shown to third parties".
what_it_sounds_like: A screenshot or document presented as something you wrote or said, that you have no memory of actually creating.
"Receipts" shown to a third party that don't match your own records of the same conversation or event.
A document or message surfaces that contains details or phrasing inconsistent with how you actually communicate.
what_it_is_not: Preserve your own originals with metadata; do not delete anything; forensic verification and defamation are legal matters — document and seek advice.
this_may_be_it_when: It fits a documented, named pattern of this kind of digital harm.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Genuine, honest misremembering happens and isn't the same as deliberate fabrication.
Authentic documents taken out of context can look misleading without being forged.
common_false_positives: A genuine misremembering on someone's part, presenting an inaccurate account sincerely rather than a deliberately forged document.
An authentic document that's simply been taken out of context, rather than fabricated outright.
Two people with a real factual disagreement where neither is fabricating anything, just remembering or interpreting events differently.
discernment_questions: Do you have your own independent record that contradicts the presented evidence?
Are there technical inconsistencies suggesting the document isn't authentic?
Does the presented material contain claims or details you can independently prove couldn't be true?
Is this a single, isolated discrepancy, or part of a broader pattern of manufactured documentation?
less_concerning_if: The discrepancy is explainable by genuine misremembering or lack of context, without evidence of deliberate fabrication.
more_concerning_if: Independent records contradict the presented material, with technical inconsistencies suggesting it isn't authentic.
existing_specific_text.repair_check: Corrective-action check: was the content taken down, the account recovered, or the false material retracted after being reported? Was there a documented resolution, or is it ongoing? Repair here looks like documentation, verification, and platform/legal response — not an apology.
existing_specific_text.boundary_respect_check: What happens when you document what occurred, report it through the appropriate channel, restrict further access, or seek outside support? Does the situation improve with those concrete steps, or does it continue regardless?
existing_specific_text.psychological_mechanism: One documented mechanism behind patterns like this is that they can operate by controlling what information the other person has access to, so their conclusions are built on an incomplete or false picture. This describes a documented mechanism at this scale, not a claim about any specific current event or actor.
existing_specific_text.possible_impact_on_receiver: People sometimes describe misplaced trust in a distorted picture of a situation, discovered later, if at all in connection with patterns like this. Impact varies widely by person, history, and context — this is a possibility to consider, not a predicted or universal outcome, and it is not a diagnosis of the person on the receiving end of a sustained pattern like this.
existing_specific_text.boundary_script: Documentation/reporting script (to a platform or authority, not the person responsible): "I want to report [specific content/account]. Here is what I have documented: [evidence]. What are my options?"
existing_specific_text.safety_note: A phrase-matching tool cannot decide safety. If this involves threats, monitoring, isolation, sex, money, housing, immigration, self-harm pressure, retaliation, or fear for safety, prioritize real-world support from a trusted person, local support service, legal/workplace resource, or emergency help if immediate danger exists. For this specific situation, prioritize evidence preservation (originals, URLs, timestamps — delete nothing) and reporting through the platform, a police cybercrime unit, or a specialized helpline over trying to resolve it through direct conversation.

members.name: Forged Screenshots
members.source_definition: Fabricated or altered digital images of conversations, messages, or documents presented as authentic proof.

approved_draft.why_this_matters: Screenshots are widely treated as settled proof, so disproving one means asking people to doubt a kind of evidence they normally accept without question.
approved_draft.what_it_is_not: A real screenshot cropped for brevity, with its meaning intact, is not a forgery. Confusion about which conversation or timeframe an image comes from is common. Different devices and platform updates genuinely produce different formatting of authentic images.

existing_specific_text.short_definition: Fabricated or altered digital images of conversations, messages, or documents presented as authentic proof.
existing_specific_text.expanded_definition: Fabricated or digitally altered images of conversations, messages, or documents, presented as authentic evidence of something that didn't actually happen or wasn't actually said. This differs from Fabricated Evidence broadly in being specifically about the digital-image medium — text message screenshots, edited photos of documents — which can be especially convincing because screenshots are widely treated as straightforward proof.
existing_specific_text.plain_language_summary: In plain terms: fabricated or altered digital images of conversations, messages, or documents presented as authentic proof.
existing_specific_text.why_this_matters: Patterns like this can shape communication, trust, and decision-making — left unnamed, they can contribute to misplaced trust in a distorted picture of a situation, discovered later, if at all. Naming a pattern accurately — without over-claiming — is usually what restores clarity faster than either ignoring it or catastrophizing it.
what_it_is: Fabricated or altered digital images of conversations, messages, or documents presented as authentic proof.
what_it_sounds_like: A screenshot presented as evidence that doesn't match the target's own records of the same conversation.
Formatting inconsistencies that don't match the messaging platform it's claimed to be from.
The alleged conversation contains claims or phrasing that don't match how the target actually communicates.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Genuine screenshots get cropped for brevity all the time without altering meaning. Confusion about which conversation a screenshot is from is a common, innocent mistake.
common_false_positives: A genuine screenshot that's simply been cropped for brevity, without altering its actual content or meaning.
Legitimate confusion about which specific conversation or timeframe a screenshot is from.
Platform updates or different devices producing genuinely different visual formatting of real screenshots.

Are there technical inconsistencies that don't match the claimed platform or device?
Is there any independent way to verify the screenshot against the original account or platform?
Does the alleged content match how the target actually writes and communicates?
less_concerning_if: The screenshot checks out against independent records and platform-consistent formatting.
more_concerning_if: The content contradicts the target's own records, and there are technical inconsistencies suggesting alteration.

members.name: Half-Truth Framing
members.source_definition: Combining true details in a way that creates a false overall impression.

approved_draft.why_this_matters: Every fact checks out individually, so a listener who verifies carefully still arrives at the wrong conclusion.
approved_draft.what_it_is_not: An accurate summary necessarily omits detail for length. People often present facts in whatever order those facts occurred to them. A genuinely different, honestly held interpretation of the same true facts is disagreement rather than arrangement.

existing_specific_text.short_definition: Combining true details in a way that creates a false overall impression.
existing_specific_text.expanded_definition: Combining individually true details in a way that creates a false overall impression — each specific fact stated can be verified as accurate, but the selection and arrangement of those facts leads to a conclusion that wouldn't hold up if all the relevant facts were included. This differs from Lying by Omission in emphasis: the mechanism here is active combination and arrangement of true pieces, not just leaving something out.
existing_specific_text.plain_language_summary: In plain terms: combining true details in a way that creates a false overall impression.
existing_specific_text.why_this_matters: Patterns like this can shape communication, trust, and decision-making — left unnamed, they can contribute to misplaced trust in a distorted picture of a situation, discovered later, if at all. Naming a pattern accurately — without over-claiming — is usually what restores clarity faster than either ignoring it or catastrophizing it.
what_it_is: Combining true details in a way that creates a false overall impression.
what_it_sounds_like: A sequence of individually accurate facts, arranged in a way that implies something the full picture wouldn't support.
Challenging the overall impression is met with "but everything I said was true," missing the point that the combination was misleading.
When additional true context is added, the original impression created by the selective combination falls apart.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Genuinely accurate summaries necessarily simplify and can't include everything. People sometimes just describe things in the order they occurred to them, without any strategic arrangement.
common_false_positives: A genuinely accurate summary that necessarily leaves out some detail simply because of length or relevance.
Someone presenting facts in the order they naturally occurred to them, without strategic arrangement.
A person with a genuinely different, honestly-held interpretation of what the same true facts mean.
discernment_questions: Does adding the missing context change the overall impression the combination created?
Is the specific combination of facts unusual, or does it reflect a natural, non-strategic way of describing the situation?
Does the person resist adding relevant context when it's offered, or readily incorporate it?
Would a neutral summary of the same facts, without the specific arrangement, support the same conclusion?
less_concerning_if: The summary holds up even with additional relevant context added.
more_concerning_if: The impression created falls apart once missing context is added, and that context is actively resisted.

members.name: Paltering
members.source_definition: Actively using literally true statements deliberately selected and arranged to create a false impression, exploiting the assumption that truthfulness equals honesty while technically never uttering a lie.

approved_draft.why_this_matters: The target is misled by statements that are all individually true, and when they object they are told, correctly, that nothing false was said — so they end up doubting their own reasonable inference rather than the account.
approved_draft.what_it_is_not: Careful, precise people answer exactly what was asked without steering anyone anywhere, and someone can answer honestly with an incomplete picture because that is all they had. There are also things people are legitimately entitled not to disclose at all.

existing_specific_text.short_definition: Actively using literally true statements deliberately selected and arranged to create a false impression, exploiting the assumption that truthfulness equals honesty while technically never uttering a lie.
existing_specific_text.expanded_definition: Actively using literally true statements, deliberately selected and arranged, to create a false overall impression — exploiting the common assumption that literal truthfulness is the same as honesty, while never technically uttering a false statement. This is closely related to Half-Truth Framing, but paltering specifically emphasizes the active, deliberate selection of true statements as a strategy, often in response to a direct question, rather than in a general narrative.
existing_specific_text.plain_language_summary: In plain terms: actively using literally true statements deliberately selected and arranged to create a false impression, exploiting the assumption that truthfulness equals honesty while technically never uttering a lie.
existing_specific_text.why_this_matters: Patterns like this can shape communication, trust, and decision-making — left unnamed, they can contribute to mental exhaustion and a loss of confidence in one's own ability to follow or hold a position in an argument. Naming a pattern accurately — without over-claiming — is usually what restores clarity faster than either ignoring it or catastrophizing it.
what_it_is: Actively using literally true statements deliberately selected and arranged to create a false impression, exploiting the assumption that truthfulness equals honesty while technically never uttering a lie.
what_it_sounds_like: A direct, specific question answered with a technically true statement that carefully avoids the actual substance being asked about.
Later confrontation about the misleading impression is met with "but everything I said was true," missing that the selection itself was misleading.
A pattern of answers that are individually accurate but collectively steer toward a false conclusion.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Precise, careful communicators sometimes just answer exactly what's asked, without any intent to mislead. People without full information sometimes give honestly incomplete answers.
common_false_positives: A genuinely careful, precise communicator who answers exactly what's asked without deliberately steering toward a false impression.
Someone who didn't have the full picture themselves and answered honestly with what they knew, which happened to be incomplete.
A person legitimately protecting sensitive information they're not obligated to share, without creating an affirmatively false impression.
discernment_questions: Does the technically-true answer, taken as a whole, create an impression that the full facts wouldn't support?
Was there a more direct, still-honest way to answer that was deliberately avoided?
Does this pattern of carefully-selected true statements recur specifically around inconvenient topics?
Would a reasonable listener, hearing the technically-true answer, walk away with an accurate understanding?
less_concerning_if: The answer, while perhaps incomplete, doesn't actively create a false impression when considered as a whole.
more_concerning_if: A pattern of carefully-selected, technically-true statements consistently creates false impressions on inconvenient topics.

related_tactics.name: Lying

related_tactics.name: Lying by Omission
related_tactics.definition: Leaving out information necessary for an accurate understanding, without technically stating anything false.

related_tactics.name: Priming / Narrative Seeding
related_tactics.definition: Subtly installing a frame before an encounter so all subsequent information gets filtered through a lens the target never consciously chose.

related_tactics.name: Frame Control
related_tactics.definition: Controlling what the conversation is "about" so the target's truth cannot survive inside the manipulator's framing.

related_tactics.name: Credibility Theft
related_tactics.definition: Undermining someone's reliability as a witness to their own experience so their testimony is pre-discounted.

related_tactics.name: Projection
related_tactics.definition: Attributing one's own harmful behavior, motives, or flaws to the target so the real source of harm is invisible.

related_tactics.name: Authority Hijack
related_tactics.definition: Claiming interpretive authority over the target's inner experience, positioning oneself as the expert on what they "really" feel or mean.

related_tactics.name: Accountability Evasion via Diagnosis
related_tactics.definition: Replacing "we failed you" with a diagnosis that makes the problem the target's condition rather than the system's behavior.

entries.name: Lying by Omission
entries.MERGED_ENTRY: The author merged these tactics into ONE entry. Write a single entry under the name 'Lying by Omission' that fully covers every member below. In expanded_definition say the others are the same tactic under different names, and name them. Draw what_it_sounds_like, what_it_is_not and the other lists from ALL members (choose the best and most distinct items; do not just concatenate). Each member's previously written entry, if there is one, is the best starting text.

members.name: Lying by Omission
members.source_definition: Leaving out information necessary for an accurate understanding, without technically stating anything false.

approved_draft.why_this_matters: Nothing said was false, so there is no untruth to point at — only a conclusion the listener reached themselves on grounds they did not know were incomplete.
approved_draft.what_it_is_not: Not thinking to mention something that did not seem relevant is ordinary, and plenty of information is legitimately nobody else's business. A gap held briefly, with a plan to close it once the timing was right, is a delay rather than a concealment.

existing_specific_text.short_definition: Leaving out information necessary for an accurate understanding, without technically stating anything false.
existing_specific_text.expanded_definition: Leaving out information necessary for an accurate understanding, without technically stating anything false. As a communication pattern, Lying by Omission-type behavior in the Deception category tends to work by controlling what information the other person has access to, so their conclusions are built on an incomplete or false picture — describing a pattern in the exchange, not a fixed trait in the person. As a Reference-only entry, note: this cannot be established from pasted text at all — it's included for learning the concept, not for detection.
existing_specific_text.plain_language_summary: In plain terms: leaving out information necessary for an accurate understanding, without technically stating anything false.
existing_specific_text.why_this_matters: Patterns like this can shape communication, trust, and decision-making — left unnamed, they can contribute to misplaced trust in a distorted picture of a situation, discovered later, if at all. Naming a pattern accurately — without over-claiming — is usually what restores clarity faster than either ignoring it or catastrophizing it.
what_it_is: Leaving out information necessary for an accurate understanding, without technically stating anything false.
what_it_sounds_like: A technically accurate account that leaves out the one piece of information that would have changed the target's decision.
"I never said that wasn't true" offered as a defense against a claim that something important was concealed.
The target discovers, later, a fact that was known to the other person the whole time and never mentioned.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People forget to mention things constantly, without any intent to deceive. Reasonable privacy about matters that aren't someone else's business isn't the same as deceptive omission.
common_false_positives: Genuinely not thinking to mention something that didn't seem relevant or important at the time.
Reasonable discretion about sharing information that's private or not the target's business.
Information that was withheld only briefly, with a plan to share it once the timing or circumstances were right.
discernment_questions: Would the omitted information have changed a decision the target made, had they known it?
Is there a plausible, non-strategic reason for the omission, or does it consistently serve the withholder's interest?
Was the information eventually shared voluntarily, or only discovered independently?
Does a pattern emerge of specifically omitting the details that would change outcomes?
less_concerning_if: The omission seems like genuine oversight, or reasonable discretion about something that wasn't the target's business.
more_concerning_if: A pattern emerges of specifically omitting exactly the information that would have changed the target's decisions.
existing_specific_text.repair_check: After the incident, was there a genuine acknowledgment (not a non-apology), a concrete change in behavior, and no repeat of the same pattern? Repair is a pattern of change over time, not a single sentence of regret.
existing_specific_text.boundary_respect_check: When a boundary was stated plainly in this area, was it honored going forward — or tested, ignored, punished, or reframed as unreasonable? Boundary respect observed over multiple instances is one of the more reliable signals available.
existing_specific_text.psychological_mechanism: One documented mechanism behind patterns like this is that they can operate by controlling what information the other person has access to, so their conclusions are built on an incomplete or false picture. This describes a possible mechanism, not a claim about what any specific person intended.
existing_specific_text.possible_impact_on_receiver: People sometimes describe misplaced trust in a distorted picture of a situation, discovered later, if at all in connection with patterns like this. Impact varies widely by person, history, and context — this is a possibility to consider, not a predicted or universal outcome, and it is not a diagnosis of the person on the receiving end of a sustained pattern like this.
existing_specific_text.safety_note: No elevated safety concern is implied by this entry on its own. If a situation ever does involve threats, monitoring, isolation, or fear for your safety, the general guidance still applies: A phrase-matching tool cannot decide safety. If this involves threats, monitoring, isolation, sex, money, housing, immigration, self-harm pressure, retaliation, or fear for safety, prioritize real-world support from a trusted person, local support service, legal/workplace resource, or emergency help if immediate danger exists.

members.name: Gaslighting by Omission
members.source_definition: Telling technical truth while deliberately withholding key context to create a fundamentally false picture, where the lie lives in what's left out.

approved_draft.why_this_matters: Decisions get made on a picture that was accurate in every detail and wrong as a whole, and the missing piece usually surfaces too late to change what was chosen.
approved_draft.what_it_is_not: Forgetting to mention a detail that did not register as important at the time is ordinary, and some people share things gradually rather than volunteering everything at once. What distinguishes the pattern is that the omitted piece is the specific one that would have changed the listener's decision.

existing_specific_text.short_definition: Telling technical truth while deliberately withholding key context to create a fundamentally false picture, where the lie lives in what's left out.
existing_specific_text.expanded_definition: Telling technical truth while deliberately withholding key context to create a fundamentally false picture, where the lie lives in what's left out. As a communication pattern, Gaslighting by Omission-type behavior in the Reality Distortion category tends to work by targeting confidence in one's own memory or perception, so the person starts checking their read of events against the other person's account instead of their own — describing a pattern in the exchange, not a fixed trait in the person. As a Reference-only entry, note: this cannot be established from pasted text at all — it's included for learning the concept, not for detection.
existing_specific_text.plain_language_summary: In plain terms: telling technical truth while deliberately withholding key context to create a fundamentally false picture, where the lie lives in what's left out.
existing_specific_text.why_this_matters: Patterns like this can shape communication, trust, and decision-making — left unnamed, they can contribute to increased self-doubt, difficulty trusting one's own memory, and a growing habit of deferring to someone else's account of events. Naming a pattern accurately — without over-claiming — is usually what restores clarity faster than either ignoring it or catastrophizing it.
what_it_is: Telling technical truth while deliberately withholding key context to create a fundamentally false picture, where the lie lives in what's left out.
what_it_sounds_like: A factually accurate account of an event that leaves out the one detail that would completely change how it's understood.
"I told you about it" turns out to mean a vague mention buried in an unrelated conversation, technically true but functionally concealing.
The target later discovers a piece of context that, had they known it earlier, would have changed their whole read of the situation.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People forget to mention things constantly without any intent to deceive. Reasonable discretion about what to share isn't the same as strategic omission.
common_false_positives: Genuinely forgetting to mention a detail that wasn't recognized as important at the time.
A person who shares information gradually and organically, not withholding it strategically, but also not volunteering everything at once.
Reasonable discretion about sharing information that isn't the target's business, without any intent to create a false impression.
discernment_questions: Does the omitted detail, once known, meaningfully change the picture the target had?
Is there a plausible reason the detail was left out that isn't strategic?
Does this happen once, or does a pattern emerge of technically-true accounts that consistently omit the same kind of detail?
Would the person have volunteered the detail if directly and specifically asked?
less_concerning_if: The omission seems like genuine oversight and the person readily fills in the gap when asked.
more_concerning_if: A pattern emerges of consistently omitting exactly the details that would change the picture, and direct questions are dodged too.
existing_specific_text.repair_check: After the incident, was there a genuine acknowledgment (not a non-apology), a concrete change in behavior, and no repeat of the same pattern? Repair is a pattern of change over time, not a single sentence of regret.
existing_specific_text.boundary_respect_check: When a boundary was stated plainly in this area, was it honored going forward — or tested, ignored, punished, or reframed as unreasonable? Boundary respect observed over multiple instances is one of the more reliable signals available.
existing_specific_text.psychological_mechanism: One documented mechanism behind patterns like this is that they can operate by targeting confidence in one's own memory or perception, so the person starts checking their read of events against the other person's account instead of their own. This describes a possible mechanism, not a claim about what any specific person intended.

Impact varies widely by person, history, and context — this is a possibility to consider, not a predicted or universal outcome, and it is not a diagnosis of the person on the receiving end of a sustained pattern like this.

members.name: Selective Information Sharing
members.source_definition: Sharing only the facts that support a preferred narrative while withholding relevant context.

approved_draft.why_this_matters: The account is accurate in every particular and still leaves the listener with a conclusion the full picture would not support.
approved_draft.what_it_is_not: Context can be missing because the speaker never had it, which is a gap rather than a filter. Sharing what you know as you learn it, across several conversations, is a different thing from choosing in advance which facts another person gets.

existing_specific_text.short_definition: Sharing only the facts that support a preferred narrative while withholding relevant context.
existing_specific_text.expanded_definition: Sharing only the specific facts that support a preferred narrative while withholding other, relevant context that would complicate or contradict it. Unlike Half-Truth Framing, which is about how true facts are arranged and combined, this is about which facts get shared at all — a filtering process that happens before any framing or combination even occurs.
existing_specific_text.plain_language_summary: In plain terms: sharing only the facts that support a preferred narrative while withholding relevant context.
existing_specific_text.why_this_matters: Patterns like this can shape communication, trust, and decision-making — left unnamed, they can contribute to misplaced trust in a distorted picture of a situation, discovered later, if at all. Naming a pattern accurately — without over-claiming — is usually what restores clarity faster than either ignoring it or catastrophizing it.
what_it_is: Sharing only the facts that support a preferred narrative while withholding relevant context.
what_it_sounds_like: A situation described using only the facts that make one interpretation look correct, with contradicting facts never mentioned.
When the withheld information surfaces from another source, it meaningfully changes how the original account should have been understood.
A consistent pattern of sharing details that favor one narrative while specific, relevant counter-details never come up.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People often genuinely don't know all the relevant context when they share their account. Reasonable summaries necessarily leave some things out without any strategic intent.
common_false_positives: Genuinely not knowing about the withheld information at the time of sharing, rather than deliberately filtering it out.
A reasonable summary that necessarily excludes some detail due to length, without strategic selection.
Sharing information gradually and organically over time, rather than in a single filtered account.
discernment_questions: Did the person plausibly have access to the withheld information at the time they shared their account?
Does the pattern of what's shared versus withheld consistently favor one particular narrative?
Does presenting the withheld context change the picture meaningfully?
Is there a plausible non-strategic reason certain details weren't mentioned?
less_concerning_if: The person plausibly didn't know the withheld information, or the omission doesn't meaningfully change the picture.
more_concerning_if: A consistent pattern emerges of specifically withholding whatever would complicate the preferred narrative.
